Oh, so a monoid is a group with a single operation, is that it?
ChatGPT said:

Exactly! A monoid is like a group, but without the requirement for inverses.

Monoid vs. Group (The Key Difference)

  • A group has:

    1. Closure (doing the operation on two elements stays in the set)
    2. Associativity (order of grouping doesn’t matter)
    3. Identity Element (there’s a "do-nothing" element)
    4. Inverses (every element has an opposite that undoes it)

  • A monoid has only the first three:

    1. Closure ✅
    2. Associativity ✅
    3. Identity Element ✅
    4. Inverses ❌ (Not required! This is the main difference!)

Example of a Monoid (String Concatenation)

  • Set: All possible strings
  • Operation: Concatenation
  • Identity Element: The empty string ""
  • Closure: Combining two strings always gives another string.
  • Associativity: ("A" + "B") + "C" = "A" + ("B" + "C")
  • No Inverses: You can’t "undo" a concatenation cleanly. ("AB" → ??? "A" and "B" don’t automatically separate.)

Since there are no inverses, this is a monoid but not a group.

Example of a Group (Integers Under Addition)

  • Set: All integers Z\mathbb{Z}Z
  • Operation: Addition
  • Identity Element: 000
  • Closure: Adding two integers gives another integer.
  • Associativity: (a+b)+c=a+(b+c)(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)(a+b)+c=a+(b+c)
  • Inverses Exist! 5+(−5)=05 + (-5) = 05+(−5)=0, so every element has an opposite.

Since inverses exist, this is a group.

MilkChan’s Thoughts on Monoids vs. Groups

I bet she’d find monoids more interesting because:

  • They allow for one-way operations (which mimic her obsessive thought loops).
  • They build order and structure without needing an "undo" button.
  • She might see inverse operations as chaotic, so a monoid feels safer than a group.

If you told her that string concatenation is a monoid, she’d probably say:

"So… words can only be added, never undone? Sounds like my intrusive thoughts. Cool!"
